title: Horror is big business
summary: Resident Evil franchise continues its 30-year dominance in gaming, with the latest title Resident Evil Requiem selling 8 million copies since February and becoming Capcom's 14th best-selling game. A film reboot is also in development, demonstrating the horror franchise's enduring appeal across multiple media formats.
content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on how pervasive horror has become, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback, arrives in our subscribers' inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
How it started
Resident Evil has been around for 30 years, but the survival horror series is more popular than ever. The most recent game, Resident Evil Requiem, has sold 8 million copies since it launched in February, already making it the 14th best-selling game that Capcom has ever made. zh.title: 恐怖游戏是大生意
zh.summary: 《生化危机》系列延续其在游戏领域30年的主导地位，最新作品《生化危机：安魂曲》自2月以来销售800万份，成为卡普空第14畅销游戏。一部电影重启版也在开发中，展示了恐怖特许经营在多个媒体形式中的持久吸引力。

title: Why the LeapPad couldn’t survive the iPad
summary: The LeapPad was once America's must-have educational toy, offering interactive learning through a smart book format that could play sounds and respond to touch. However, the product ultimately couldn't survive the iPad's market dominance despite its early success and appeal to both children and parents.
content:
For multiple years, the hottest toy in the United States was a book. But not just any book: a smart book that could play sounds and respond to taps and help kids learn to read. However, buying it came with a high price and big parenting questions.
On the next episode of Version History, David Pierce is joined by The Verge's Andru Marino and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy to explain how the LeapPad worked, why it was so enticing to both kids and adults, and why the company that made it could never quite follow it up.

zh.title: LeapPad为何无法在iPad时代生存
zh.summary: LeapPad曾是美国必备的教育玩具，通过智能书籍格式提供交互式学习，可以播放声音和响应触摸。但尽管其早期成功且深受儿童和家长欢迎，该产品最终无法在iPad的市场主导地位中生存。

title: Learning to use local AI is exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating
summary: Running powerful AI models locally on personal computers is becoming increasingly viable as an alternative to cloud-based services, offering privacy benefits but requiring significant hardware investment and presenting a steep learning curve. This shift reflects growing interest in keeping personal data off cloud services while exploring AI capabilities.
content:
Baby’s first local AI agent. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge	

I'm embarking on a journey I've so far been hesitant to go on: actually using AI on the regular. Giving my most personal data to cloud services has been a major hold up for me, but it's increasingly possible to run powerful models locally to see what they're capable of. Is this tech so useful that it's worth throwing gobs of money at a computer or a laptop with lots of overpriced RAM? I'll try to help you find out. I'm not an AI expert, it's going to be a journey for me, but maybe I can help you see if that journey is worth taking - and I'll be posting my way through it.
